Despondency
dē-spŏn´dĕn-sy
n. (dejection at the loss of hope; a sinking of the spirit that stops short of despair)
Latin despondere, to give up, to promise away — the same verb used of pledging a daughter in marriage. To despond is to hand one's hope over to someone else's keeping and give up the claim.

Biblical Definition

Despondency is the sinking of hope. The psalmist interrogates it rather than denying it: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him” (Psa 42:5). Elijah, the day after Carmel, asks to die: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers” (1Ki 19:4). Paul distinguishes it from ruin: “we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair” (2Co 4:8). The psalm names the failure and the remedy together: “My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever” (Psa 73:26). And Lamentations turns on a deliberate act of memory (Lam 3:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines despondency as a sinking or dejection of spirit at the loss of hope; and despond as to be cast down, to lose hope and confidence, to sink by loss of courage.

expand to see more

DESPONDENCY, n. A sinking or dejection of spirit at the loss of hope; loss of courage at the failure of hope, or in deep affliction, or at the prospect of insurmountable difficulties.

DESPOND, v.i. To be cast down; to be depressed or dejected in mind; to fail in spirits.

The unfortunate man despondeth, and gives up all hope of relief.

Key Scripture

Psa 42:5 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."

1Ki 19:4 — "But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers."

2Co 4:8 — "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;"

Psa 73:26 — "My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever."

Lam 3:21 — "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope."

Modern Corruption

Despondency is treated as unbelief and shamed, and God's response to Elijah under the juniper tree was food and sleep.

expand to see more

First Kings 19 should govern how the church handles this, because it is God's own bedside manner with a man in the worst state of his life. Elijah has just won the most spectacular victory in the Old Testament and forty days later he is under a juniper tree asking to die. There is no rebuke. An angel touches him and says arise and eat; he eats and sleeps, and is fed a second time, because the journey is too great for thee. Only afterwards, at Horeb, comes the question and the still small voice and the correction of his facts — he was not the only one left; there were seven thousand. Food, sleep, gentleness, and only then the theology.

Psalm 42 shows the internal work, and its method is neither suppression nor indulgence. The psalmist addresses his own soul: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? — a question, which assumes the state is real and that reasons can be asked for. Then a command: hope thou in God. Then a fact about the future: for I shall yet praise him. He is preaching to himself rather than listening to himself, and the psalm ends without the feeling having lifted, which is why it is trustworthy.

Lamentations 3:21 identifies the hinge and it is a verb of choice: This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. The chapter before it is unrelieved — he has led me into darkness, he hath set me in dark places as they that be dead of old — and nothing in the circumstances changes at verse 21. What changes is what he calls to mind: the mercies of the LORD, that they are new every morning. Hope in Scripture is not the absence of despondency but a deliberate act performed inside it, and it is available to a man who cannot feel anything at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachach (H7817), to be bowed down; hamah (H1993), to be disquieted, in tumult; Greek exaporeomai (G1820), to be utterly without a way, in despair; aporeomai (G639), to be perplexed.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachach (H7817) — to be cast down, bowed; Psalm 42:5, 42:11, 43:5.

Greek aporoumenoi all' ouk exaporoumenoi (G639, G1820) — perplexed, but not in despair; 2 Corinthians 4:8 — a play on the same root.

Hebrew chesed YHWH (H2617) — the mercies of the LORD; Lamentations 3:22–23.

Usage

"“Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee” — and no rebuke."

"“Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” — preaching to himself, not listening."

"“This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope” — a verb of choice."
